title: The Wonderful World of Science
description: Grade 6 Science: what science is, scientific thinking, observation vs inference, and the steps of the scientific method — notes, solved examples and a practice test.

topics.title: Introduction to Scientific Thinking
topics.concept:
Science is a way of understanding the world by asking questions and looking for answers through evidence — not by simply guessing or believing. The word comes from the Latin scientia, meaning ‘knowledge’.

Science begins with curiosity. Why is the sky blue? Why does ice float on water? How do birds fly? A scientist is anyone who notices something, wonders about it, and then tries to find out why or how it happens.

Scientific thinking has a few habits that you can practise every day:

  • Be curious — ask ‘why’, ‘how’ and ‘what if’ about everyday things.
  • Look for evidence — accept an idea only when there is proof for it.
  • Keep an open mind — be ready to change your idea if new evidence shows it is wrong.
  • Be honest — record exactly what you see, even if it is not what you expected.

Science is not only done in laboratories by people in white coats. A cook adjusting a recipe, a farmer choosing the best seeds, and a child working out which paper plane flies farthest are all using scientific thinking.

examples.problem: Example 1: Riya believes that plants grow better when you talk to them. How can she turn this belief into a scientific question worth testing?
examples.solution:
A belief becomes science when it can be tested with evidence.

  • Rephrase it as a clear question: ‘Do plants that are spoken to every day grow taller than plants that are not?’
  • Plan a fair test: two similar plants, same pot, soil, water and sunlight — one is spoken to, one is not.
  • Measure and compare their heights after a few weeks.
examples.answer: She should turn the belief into a testable question and compare two similar plants under identical conditions, changing only whether they are spoken to.

examples.problem: Example 2: Give one reason why ‘Mangoes taste better than apples’ is not a scientific statement.
examples.solution:
Science deals with claims that can be checked by everyone with evidence.

  • Taste is a matter of personal opinion — it is different for each person.
  • There is no measurement or experiment that can prove it true or false for everyone.
examples.answer: It is a personal opinion, not a fact, so it cannot be tested or proved with evidence.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name two everyday activities, outside a laboratory, where people use scientific thinking.
examples.solution:
Scientific thinking is used whenever someone observes, tries something and checks the result.

  • A cook tasting food and adjusting the salt until it is right.
  • A cricketer changing how they hold the ball to make it swing.
examples.answer: Examples include a cook adjusting a recipe by tasting, or a cricketer changing grip to swing the ball — both observe, try and check.

recap:
• Science is knowledge gained by asking questions and finding answers through evidence, not guesses.
  • It begins with curiosity — asking why and how things happen.
  • Scientific thinking means being curious, looking for evidence, keeping an open mind and being honest.
  • A scientific statement can be tested; a personal opinion cannot.

quiz.explanation: Science accepts an idea only when there is evidence and it can be tested.

quiz.q: Which of these is a scientific question?
options: Is maths more fun than music?
Does a heavier ball roll down a slope faster?
quiz.explanation: Only the rolling-ball question can be answered by observation and measurement; the others are opinions.

topics.title: Observations and Experiments
topics.concept:
An observation is information you gather using your senses (sight, hearing, smell, touch, taste) or with instruments. ‘The liquid turned blue’ and ‘the bell rang twice’ are observations.

An inference is a conclusion you draw from an observation. If you observe that the ground is wet (observation), you might infer that it rained (inference). Notice that an inference can be wrong — perhaps someone washed the street. Good scientists are careful to keep the two apart.

Observations are of two kinds:

  • Qualitative — describes a quality, with no numbers. Example: ‘the flame is yellow’.
  • Quantitative — uses a number and a unit, by measuring. Example: ‘the rod is 30 cm long’. Quantitative observations are more precise and easier to compare.

An experiment is a carefully planned test that we do to answer a question. In a fair test, we change only one thing at a time (called the variable) and keep everything else the same. This way, if the result changes, we know exactly what caused it.

Scientists use tools to observe more carefully than the senses allow — a ruler for length, a balance for mass, a thermometer for temperature, a hand lens or microscope to see tiny things, and a measuring cylinder for the volume of liquids.

examples.problem: Example 1: Sort these into observation or inference: (a) The leaf is green. (b) The plant must be healthy.
examples.solution:
An observation uses the senses directly; an inference is a conclusion drawn from it.

  • (a) ‘The leaf is green’ — this is seen directly, so it is an observation.
  • (b) ‘The plant must be healthy’ — this is a conclusion based on the colour, so it is an inference.
examples.answer: (a) is an observation; (b) is an inference.

examples.problem: Example 2: Rewrite the qualitative observation ‘the water is hot’ as a quantitative observation.
examples.solution:
A quantitative observation needs a number and a unit, which means we must measure.

  • Use a thermometer to measure the temperature.
  • State it with a number and unit, for example: ‘the water is at 65°C’.
examples.answer: Measure with a thermometer and state it as, for example, ‘the water is at 65°C’.

examples.problem: Example 3: A student wants to find out if fertiliser makes a plant grow taller. To make it a fair test, what should she keep the same and what should she change?
examples.solution:
In a fair test only the variable being studied is changed.

  • Change (variable): whether fertiliser is added.
  • Keep the same: the type of plant, pot size, amount of soil, water, sunlight and temperature.
examples.answer: Change only the fertiliser; keep the plant type, soil, water, sunlight and all other conditions identical.

recap:
• An observation is gathered with the senses or instruments; an inference is a conclusion drawn from observations and can be wrong.
  • Qualitative observations describe a quality; quantitative observations use a number and a unit.
  • An experiment is a planned test; a fair test changes only one variable and keeps everything else the same.
  • Tools such as the ruler, balance, thermometer, hand lens and measuring cylinder help us observe accurately.

quiz.q: ‘The sky is cloudy, so it will probably rain’ — the second part of this sentence is an:
quiz.explanation: Predicting rain is a conclusion drawn from the observation of clouds, so it is an inference.

quiz.q: Which of these is a quantitative observation?
options: The box has a mass of 2 kg
quiz.explanation: A quantitative observation has a number and a unit, such as 2 kg.

quiz.q: In a fair test, how many things should you change at one time?
quiz.explanation: Changing only one variable lets you be sure what caused any change in the result.

topics.title: The Scientific Method
topics.concept:
The scientific method is a step-by-step way of answering a question with evidence. It is not a rigid set of rules but a sensible cycle that scientists follow, often repeating steps as they learn more.

  • 1. Ask a question — based on something you observed. e.g. ‘Does sugar dissolve faster in hot water than in cold water?’
  • 2. Make a hypothesis — a possible answer you can test, usually an ‘if…then…’ idea. e.g. ‘If the water is hotter, then the sugar will dissolve faster.’
  • 3. Plan and do an experiment — a fair test that changes only one variable.
  • 4. Observe and record — note the results carefully, often in a table.
  • 5. Draw a conclusion — decide whether the results support the hypothesis.
  • 6. Communicate — share what you found so others can check and build on it.

A hypothesis is a smart, testable guess — not a final answer. If the experiment does not support it, that is still a success: the scientist learns something and forms a better hypothesis. This is why being wrong is a normal and useful part of science.

Repeating an experiment and getting the same result makes us more confident. A result that can be repeated by others is called reproducible, and reproducibility is one of the things that makes science trustworthy.

examples.problem: Example 1: Arrange these steps of the scientific method in the correct order: conclusion, question, experiment, hypothesis.
examples.solution:
Recall the cycle: a question comes first, then a testable guess, then a test, then a conclusion.

  • Question → Hypothesis → Experiment → Conclusion.

examples.problem: Example 2: Write a testable hypothesis for the question: ‘Does a paper plane with a pointed nose fly farther than one with a flat nose?’
examples.solution:
A hypothesis is an ‘if…then…’ statement that can be tested.

  • It must clearly predict an outcome you can measure.

Hypothesis: ‘If a paper plane has a pointed nose, then it will fly a greater distance than one with a flat nose.’
examples.answer: If a paper plane has a pointed nose, then it will fly farther than one with a flat nose.

examples.problem: Example 3: An experiment does not support a student’s hypothesis. Has the experiment failed? Explain.
examples.solution:
Science treats every clear result as useful.

  • The experiment still gave a real answer — it showed the hypothesis was wrong.
  • The student can now form a better hypothesis and test again.
examples.answer: No. A result that does not support the hypothesis is still valuable; it teaches us something and leads to a better hypothesis.

recap:
• The scientific method is a cycle: question → hypothesis → experiment → observe/record → conclusion → communicate.
  • A hypothesis is a testable ‘if…then…’ guess, not a final answer.
  • If results do not support the hypothesis, that is still useful — it leads to a better idea.
  • A result that others can repeat is reproducible, which makes science trustworthy.

quiz.q: In the scientific method, a testable ‘if…then…’ guess is called a:
quiz.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction made before the experiment.

quiz.q: Which step comes immediately AFTER doing the experiment?
quiz.explanation: After the experiment, you carefully observe and record the results before drawing a conclusion.

quiz.q: A result is called reproducible when:
options: Others repeating it get the same result
quiz.explanation: Reproducible means the same result is obtained when the experiment is repeated, which builds trust in the finding.

questions.q: Science is best described as:
options: A set of facts to memorise
Gaining knowledge through questions and evidence
questions.explanation: Science is a way of building knowledge using questions and evidence.

questions.q: Which of the following is an observation?
questions.explanation: Seeing that the leaf is green is direct sensory information, so it is an observation.

questions.q: Which of these is an inference?
questions.explanation: Concluding that it rained from the wet road is an inference.

questions.q: ‘The wire is 25 cm long’ is a:
questions.explanation: It has a number and a unit, so it is a quantitative observation.

questions.q: A testable possible answer made before an experiment is a:
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a testable prediction.

questions.q: In a fair test you should change:
questions.explanation: Changing only one variable shows exactly what caused any change.

questions.q: Which instrument would you use to measure the temperature of water?
questions.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature.

questions.q: Which instrument measures the volume of a liquid?
questions.explanation: A measuring cylinder measures liquid volume.

questions.q: The correct order of the scientific method is:
questions.explanation: We ask a question, form a hypothesis, do an experiment, then conclude.

questions.q: If an experiment does not support the hypothesis, a scientist should:
options: Learn from it and form a better hypothesis
questions.explanation: Honest scientists treat an unexpected result as useful and improve their hypothesis.

questions.q: A result that others can repeat and obtain again is called:
questions.explanation: Reproducible results build trust in a scientific finding.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a habit of good scientific thinking?
options: Refusing to change your mind even with new proof
questions.explanation: Good scientists keep an open mind and update ideas when new evidence appears.

questions.q: Which statement can be tested scientifically?
options: Ice melts faster in warm water than cold water
questions.explanation: The melting of ice can be observed and measured; the others are opinions.

questions.q: A hand lens or microscope is used to:
options: See very small things more clearly
questions.explanation: Lenses magnify tiny objects so we can observe them in detail.

questions.q: The last step of the scientific method, sharing your findings, is called:
questions.explanation: Communicating results lets others check and build on the work.

questions.q: Two plants are kept in identical pots, soil, water and sunlight; only one is given plant food. This setup is designed mainly to:
options: Make a fair test by changing only one variable
questions.explanation: Keeping everything the same except the plant food makes it a fair test.

questions.q: A student measures a rod three times and gets 20.1 cm, 20.0 cm and 20.2 cm. Repeating the measurement mainly helps to:
options: Reduce mistakes and check the result is reliable
questions.explanation: Repeating measurements and getting close values shows the result is reliable.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched as observation → inference?
options: The grass is wet → it rained last night
It rained → the grass is green
The dog is brown → the dog is brown
It is morning → the time is 7 o’clock
questions.explanation: Wet grass is observed; rain is inferred from it.

questions.q: A hypothesis differs from a conclusion because a hypothesis is made:
options: After the experiment, using the results
Before the experiment, as a testable prediction
questions.explanation: A hypothesis is a prediction made before testing; a conclusion comes after.

questions.q: Which question is the MOST scientific because it can be measured?
options: Does salt water boil at a higher temperature than plain water?
questions.explanation: Boiling temperature can be measured and compared; the others are opinions.

questions.q: Why do scientists communicate their results to others?
options: So others can check, repeat and build on the findings
questions.explanation: Sharing allows others to reproduce the work, which makes science reliable.
